items.content:
OpenWorker -- an open source agent that doesn't just chat but completes tasks on your laptop -- just released a new version with many features for security workflows. 

After our initial release, many users found it especially useful for cybersecurity. Attackers are already using AI; OpenWorker is committed to giving defenders the same leverage. Running an agent requires both (i) A model and (ii) A harness (the software around the model). Because the OpenWorker harness is fully open source, security teams can audit it to make sure we haven't built any backdoors that exfiltrate your code and data to some company or even a foreign adversary.

OpenWorker now comes with built-in cybersecurity agents for (i) Scanning your code for vulnerabilities. (ii) Scanning dependencies for supply chain injections. (iii) Checking your cloud security configuration for attack surfaces. This enables developers to do much more security work before deployment (part of what's called the "shift left" movement).

You choose the model: you can run open weight models fully locally so sensitive code never leaves your machine. This helps with legitimate security work (like reproducing a known exploit to defend against it) that can trigger refusals in leading closed models. Or use your ChatGPT subscription, or stealth preview models like Ox Alpha, or any model via API key.

Thanks also to all the open source contributors!

Excited to see @Reuters cover the launch of our startup Accelerated Understanding.

We are training ...
items.content:
Excited to see @Reuters cover the launch of our startup Accelerated Understanding.

We are training large scale AI models that can simulate and understand physics to invent and discover. Our models understand the world directly in 4D (3D + time) and across physical phenomena. Going full 4D requires massive context length, we have pushed it to a Trillion in training and exceeding 5 Trillion at inference.

AI giving you a bigger haystack of ideas doesn’t help. The bottleneck for new inventions and discoveries is shifting from ideas to the ability to test them. With AI that can simulate and understand physics we are directly attacking this bottleneck.

People have been trying to do this for a while now, but usually by taking shortcuts. Narrow surrogates are great if you happen to have enough of precisely the right data and your design loop stays in distribution. Video models look fantastic but sweep physical accuracy under the rug, and some static world models cut out physics altogether. A lot of interesting physics isn’t visual.

What does not cutting corners look like? Space stays 3D and you also have time: so 4D in total. You also need multiple physical modalities in the same model, not just things you can see. That’s what we’ve built.

Scaling is the primary ingredient to make this work. To represent the world you need sufficient context, which in our case grows in 4 dimensions. Individual samples get so big they don’t fit into single accelerators or even full nodes anymore.

We’ve developed architectural tricks to make it work. We’ve pushed our models to 1T parameters during large scale pre-training and are able to train at up to a Trillion context when needed and do inference exceeding 5 Trillion context without any sub-sampling or patching.

Building on prior successes of AI weather forecasting, fusion simulation, design of medical devices, drugs and chips, we wanted to see if scale and universality can benefit AI for physical understanding. With our teams’ experience in large-scale infrastructure and model training we’ve been able to pull it off.

items.title: Long-context recurrent models are attractive because they can summarize everything seen so far into ...
items.content:
Long-context recurrent models are attractive because they can summarize everything seen so far into a fixed-size internal state, but that efficiency creates a problem: when a token first arrives, the model does not yet know which details a later task will need, so useful information may be compressed away.

The authors of this paper from @MIT_CSAIL propose “dynamic compression”: keep the original sequence available, and once the current task reveals what matters, selectively revisit relevant earlier tokens and process them again through the recurrent network, effectively rewriting its compact working memory around the present need.

In a controlled experiment where the model must remember and later reuse several learned functions, this extra computation greatly reduces the internal state needed for accurate reuse; with three functions, a dynamically rescanning model with about 111,000 state elements achieves lower error than a single-pass model with about 3.1 million.

Learn from the paper with an AI tutor: https://t.co/TiA2TrlbtH

items.title: Many scientific models can generate realistic data without giving a usable formula for how probable ...
items.content:
Many scientific models can generate realistic data without giving a usable formula for how probable an observation is under a particular choice of model parameters, which makes ordinary parameter estimation difficult even when the simulator itself is accurate.

This paper from @uclouvain, @ELLISInst_Tue, @MPI_IS, and @UniversiteLiege develops a clear route from that problem to simulation-based inference: using simulated examples to train neural networks that approximate the statistical quantities needed for inference.

It explains both Bayesian inference, where one estimates a posterior—a probability distribution over parameter values after seeing the data—and frequentist inference, where the goal is to construct procedures with reliable long-run error rates, then shows how the same machine-learning ideas fit into both.

items.content: The fact that Simile’s first technical blog post is about confidence is notable.  Confidence  is paramount to simulation. If a coding agent messes up, you can often tell and repair. If a simulation is wrong, you might never know and make a bad consequential decision based on it. We do rigorous evals of our simulation model, but this only tells you how well your model is going to do on average over some population + use case. The confidence model tells you how well your model is performing on each query in real-time.

I interviewed Sundar Pichai, and he made an interesting prediction for where we'll be in 3 years:

"...
items.content:
I interviewed Sundar Pichai, and he made an interesting prediction for where we'll be in 3 years:

"Any content can go from any modality to any modality. It doesn't matter how the content was originally created -- people can consume it in many different forms."

"I'm very confident three years from now you will look back at what we have today and realize it was pretty primitive. It's like looking at a flip phone."

For example, YouTube clips become blogs, newsletters become podcasts without recording.

In this world, consumers would choose the format, and creators just supply the ideas, brand, and personality.

Net-net, I think this is a good thing for content.

It kills the "more content" strategy because when anyone can produce everything, volume stops being an advantage. So, the creators who win will focus on quality.

People confuse slop with AI, but they're not the same thing. Plenty of creators already use AI in their workflows and get zero hate -- people just don't realize it. Also, YouTube's new policies target slop, not AI.

If the content is good, people don't care how it was made.

I’ve been meaning to do a longer post on token caps, so ...
items.content:
Uber really set the tone for token spend. 

I’ve been meaning to do a longer post on token caps, so here is what I’m hearing. 

Multiple F500 and DNBs have been copying Uber’s strategy of monthly limits this past quarter. 

Uber set a $1500/mo limit. 

According to several online threads:
- Fanatics caps at $3k/mo
- Coursera started enforcing limits this past quarter ranging from $75 to $2k/mo based on team and role
- T-Mobile is $2k/mo 

But then you’ve also got an employee at Walmart sharing that they spend $6k/mo with no issue. 

Even heard that Yelp not only is setting a $1000-1500 per month cap, but that whatever dollar amount the employee DOESN’T use, they get to keep it as a bonus 😮

That only works if you’re appropriately measuring output or else you’re just encouraging people to never use AI. 

You have to think about goals and incentives.  

Especially with these spend limits in place. companies need a process for uncovering AI superusers and people pushing the frontier. 

Any employee that wants to spend more than your monthly limit, you should require that they fill out an intake form with their reason and use cases. Require they share whether they attempted that use case with smaller models or open source. If you’re a small business, require a short chat with the most AI-fluent person at the company to get approval. 

Docusign is one company that employees online have shared have that exact approval process. 

You’re adding friction, but what you’re really doing is uncovering the best usage across the company. 

The interviews are data - you want to protect the P&L but not stifle innovation. 

Related: your A players will quit if you don’t let them push the boundaries of their work.

items.content:
What do I want in AI?

Here are just a few things. 

I want voice-enabled everything. 
I want things to be more proactive. 
I want to manage AI’s escalations (versus delegation). 
I want those escalations to be nicely designed and not in a boring chat. 
I don’t want to keep my laptop open. 
I want my M4 Max to stop crapping out because of my AI workloads. 
I want hundreds of VMs spun up on demand. 
I want AI to be more goal-oriented. 
I want smarter routing. 
I want to never think about compaction. 
I want AI that doesn’t sound condescending in emails and designs. 
I want designs that don’t have idiotic eyebrow text in every single section (hi Claude!). 
I want AI to not write “quiet” in everything and require me to make skills just to remove absurd-sounding AI phrases when I’m just asking for a grammar check. 
I want layered designs that look like images and not code. 
I want my conversations to be better named (Codex, looking at you!). 
I want labs to share use cases that aren’t meal prep and travel. 
I want reliable AI that can make doctor’s appointments. 
And hair appointments. 
And nails. 
All appointments, actually. 
I want AI to not write 6 paragraphs back at me, when that reply only needed one line. 
I want MCPs to stop breaking. 
I want AI to have a wake word. 
I want AI that scores itself harshly. 
I want AI to want to make things fun. 
I want more multiplayer AI. 
I want to be able to blend my Claude with someone else’s Claude (like model fusion, but agent fusion). 

These are a few of my favorite things.

Small startups might...
items.content:
I have several friends who work at an ad agency, and they aren't scared of AI.

Small startups might be okay publishing ad slop videos online, but no respectable company wants to be associated with AI-generated videos.

I've worked with Icon before. They were going after ad agencies with AI, but now their website claims their work is 100% real.

Here is the thing:

You might use a model to generate 1000 videos overnight. These videos will look good, with proper lip sync, product framing, b-roll, and perfect scripts, but someone still has to review them:

1. Does the script sound like something a real person would say?
2. Does the voice match the person on screen?
3. Does the claim sound like something a customer would believe?
4. Does the hook stop someone from scrolling?

You need people to do this.

That's what Icon realized. They still sell their AI workflow for writing, analytics, and finding promising angles, but now they use real humans in front of the camera to create the final videos.

Thanks to the Icon team for partnering with me on this post.

items.content:
Everyone needs an AI brain, these two lay out.

Theirs caught my attention because their database, or "brain," has a subconscious. In other words, over time, the brain itself stores things in long-term memory better than anything else I have been shown so far. 

This has deep implications for everything we are about to do with AI. Even when getting into an autonomous car, if it knows more about you, it will serve you better. 

These two, cofounder/CEO, Prakshal Jain, and Alex Morris cofounder laid out why their approach will:

• Hallucinate a lot less, if at all
• Be faster to run
• Be cheaper to run

This works whether you have a personal brain on your own account, or a company brain that watches your business work by rolling up context from each individual machine. 

While this is very scary new technology for people, the sheer cost advantage is what really got my attention when visiting this company in San Francisco: https://t.co/qRuIKvWtb4

Even though we will argue about the privacy implications, which we cover at depth in this interview.

Here is the future of agentic systems.

Everyone needs an AI brain, these two lay out.

Theirs caught my attention because their database, or "brain," has a subconscious. In other words, over time, the brain itself stores things in long-term memory better than anything else I have been shown so far.

This has deep implications for everything we are about to do with AI. Even when getting into an autonomous car, if it knows more about you, it will serve you better.

These two, cofounder/CEO, Prakshal Jain, and Alex Morris cofounder laid out why their approach will:

• Hallucinate a lot less, if at all

• Be faster to run

• Be cheaper to run

This works whether you have a personal brain on your own account, or a company brain that watches your business work by rolling up context from each individual machine.

While this is very scary new technology for people, the sheer cost advantage is what really got my attention when visiting this company in San Francisco: https://t.co/qRuIKvWtb4

Even though we will argue about the privacy implications, which we cover at depth in this interview.

Here is the future of agentic systems.
